title: Homiletics
description: The theology and practice of preaching. Students study the biblical basis and history of preaching, the preacher's character and calling, the movement from exegesis to sermon, sermon structure, illustration, application, delivery, and preaching different genres, the Christ-centered sermon, and preaching for different occasions. Drawing on Augustine's On Christian Doctrine Book IV, Chrysostom, Gregory the Great and Spurgeon's Lectures to My Students, students write and receive feedback on full sermon manuscripts.

quiz_bank.question: What is the theological significance of preaching?

quiz_bank.question: How should narrative texts be preached?
quiz_bank.answer_key: Retell the story vividly, follow the plot's tension and resolution, identify the narrator's theological point (what God is doing), connect to the larger redemptive story, and apply its main idea rather than moralizing details.

quiz_bank.question: Compare manuscript and extemporaneous delivery.
quiz_bank.answer_key: Manuscripts give precision and careful wording but can reduce eye contact and spontaneity; extemporaneous (from notes or memory after full preparation) gives freshness and connection but risks imprecision; many preachers write a manuscript and then preach from notes.

quiz_bank.question: Why is clarity so important in preaching?
quiz_bank.answer_key: The purpose is to communicate God's word so that hearers understand, believe and obey; unclear preaching fails its purpose (Augustine; 1 Cor 14:9).

quiz_bank.question: What elements belong in an evangelistic sermon?
quiz_bank.answer_key: A clear presentation of God, sin, Christ's death and resurrection, and the call to repent and believe; answering objections; urgency and warmth; an explicit invitation - all grounded in a biblical text.
